title: Improved heterologous protein production by a tripeptidyl peptidase gene (AosedD) disruptant of the filamentous fungus Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Zhu L; Nemoto T; Yoon J; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
journal: Journal of General and Applied Microbiology
summary: The fungus produces enzymes called proteases that can break down the proteins we want it to make. Researchers disabled a gene called AosedD to reduce that breakdown, then measured chymosin (used to make cheese) and human lysozyme (an antibacterial protein). Both products increased without an obvious growth problem.

title: Enhanced production and secretion of heterologous proteins by the filamentous fungus Aspergillus oryzae via disruption of vacuolar protein sorting receptor gene Aovps10
authors: Yoon J; Aishan T; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Some newly made proteins get sent to the fungus's internal recycling compartment instead of being released outside the cell. Researchers disrupted Aovps10, a gene involved in that routing, then measured chymosin (used to make cheese) and human lysozyme. More of both proteins reached the culture liquid, without an obvious growth defect.

title: Double disruption of the proteinase genes, tppA and pepE, increases the production level of human lysozyme by Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Jin FJ; Watanabe T; Juvvadi PR; Maruyama J; Arioka M; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers tested genes involved in breaking down unwanted proteins to see which ones limited production of human lysozyme. Disabling tppA and pepE together helped more than either change alone. But combining tppA with palB did worse than either individual edit, showing that useful changes can interfere with one another.
notes: Cargo copy number not verified in any experiment.

title: Enhanced production of bovine chymosin by autophagy deficiency in the filamentous fungus Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Yoon J; Kikuma T; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Cells have a recycling process called autophagy that can also destroy proteins they are being engineered to make. Researchers disrupted five recycling genes and measured chymosin, an enzyme used to make cheese. Several edits increased output, but others did not, and many strains had trouble making spores needed to start new cultures. They then tested adjustable gene switches to improve spore formation while retaining some of the production gains.
notes: Which strain served as the control is unclear: the text names SlD-AKC1, which has a different genetic background from the deletion strains, and the better-matched candidate in Table 1 has a genotype that contradicts its own name and parent.

title: Disruption of ten protease genes in the filamentous fungus Aspergillus oryzae highly improves production of heterologous proteins
authors: Yoon J; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers disabled more and more of the fungus's protein-destroying genes, eventually building a strain with ten of them switched off. They measured chymosin, an enzyme used to make cheese, at three successive stages and found that production rose at each one. Human lysozyme also increased in the final strain. Chymosin broke down less as the culture aged, helping explain the benefit.
notes: P5, P7, P9 and P10 are the paper's names for strains carrying that many protease deletions, each built by adding deletions to the one before. The P5 controls carry the same five deletions as the P7-P10 lineage but are a different clone. Less chymosin was lost to degradation between days 4 and 5 as deletions accumulated: 22% (P5), 5% (P7), 1% (P9), 2.5% (P10). The 84.4 mg/L P5 control is the same measurement Yoon 2009 reports, not a new one.

title: Further enhanced production of heterologous proteins by double-gene disruption (ΔAosedD ΔAovps10) in a hyper-producing mutant of Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Zhu L; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers combined ways to protect a manufactured protein: disabling an enzyme that breaks proteins down and disrupting a route that sends them into the cell's recycling compartment. They tested those changes in an already productive fungal strain making chymosin (used to make cheese) or human lysozyme. The combined changes improved production, showing that different engineering strategies can work together.
notes: AUT1 already carries ΔtppA and ΔpepE plus an uncharacterized aut1 mutation. Table 1 uses AFLN labels for HLY strains while Figs. 3c and 4c use HLY labels; the Fig. 3c control HLY6 is absent from Table 1. The abstract's headline comparison is the double disruptant against the plain AUT1 parent, about 1.6x CHY and 2.1x HLY; no single row holds it because each experiment here is read against its own intermediate parent.

title: Construction of quintuple protease gene disruptant for heterologous protein production in Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Yoon J; Kimura S; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers added more deletions of protein-destroying genes to a fungus already missing some of them. The resulting strain released more chymosin, the enzyme used to make cheese, than its starting strain. It also became a useful starting point for later studies that disabled additional protease genes.

title: Monitoring global gene expression of proteases and improvement of human lysozyme production in the nptB gene disruptant of Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Kimura S; Maruyama J; Takeuchi M; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers measured which protein-destroying enzyme genes were active while the fungus was growing, rather than choosing one to remove at random. They disrupted a gene called nptB and measured human lysozyme production. Some modified strains produced more, but the gains were modest and not consistent across strains.
notes: All HLY amounts are read from Fig. 4; the text gives only the 22% increase for the second disruptant at day 4. Fig. 4 shows means and SE of four independent experiments.

title: Two-step engineering of food-grade Aspergillus oryzae via endogenous signal peptides and vesicle trafficking proteins to enhance carrier-free protein secretion
authors: Panchanawaporn S; Rattanaphan N; Jeennor S; Anantayanon J; Woraprayote W; Pumpuang L; Karirat T; Prompakdee N; Laoteng K; Chutrakul C
summary: Proteins travel through cells in tiny packages that need help moving and joining together. Researchers made a food-grade strain of the fungus produce extra amounts of several transport-helper proteins, then measured a glowing test protein called GFP. The most promising change also improved the release of kappa-casein, a milk protein. The study also tested changes to the protein's export signal and the growth medium.
notes: Host is A. oryzae BCC7051, not a RIB40 derivative, so gene IDs are BCC7051 accessions rather than AO090 locus tags (Aosly1 OOO06293.1, Aobet1 OOO11641.1, Aosso1 OOO07523.1, Aosec1 OOO07634.1). GFP results average six independent transformants. EXCLUDED_CONSTRUCT:SIGNAL_PEPTIDE: Compared three signal peptides with no signal peptide for GFP, and tested SPAoalp1 for kappa-casein. Terminator in the overexpression cassettes is TODO because Table S1 and Figs. S2-S3 disagree. EXCLUDED_PROCESS:MEDIUM: Doubling the yeast extract in the growth medium raised kappa-casein from 0.27 to 4.14 mg/L, about 15x.

title: Extracellular Production of Neoculin, a Sweet-Tasting Heterodimeric Protein with Taste-Modifying Activity, by Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Nakajima K; Asakura T; Maruyama J; Morita Y; Oike H; Shimizu-Ibuka A; Misaka T; Sorimachi H; Arai S; Kitamoto K; Abe K
summary: Neoculin is a sweet-tasting plant protein made of two parts that must join correctly. Researchers engineered the fungus to make and release both parts, then increased activity of hacA, a gene that helps cells cope with the stress of folding proteins. That further increased neoculin production, and the resulting protein retained its sweetening activity.
notes: Fig. 2 reports averages across eight hacA transformants against one control; individual clone values are not given. Table 1 names the NBS plasmid pA3GB while the Results text calls it pA3GAB. hacA cDNA is GenBank AB246349, not an AO090 locus tag. EXCLUDED_CONSTRUCT:CLEAVAGE_LINKER: Added a triglycine linker after the KEX2 cleavage site to improve processing [Table 1; Fig. 1; Results]. EXCLUDED_CONSTRUCT:PLASMID_RATIO: Varied the amounts of the two subunit plasmids to obtain correctly assembled neoculin [Results]. EXCLUDED_CONSTRUCT:CONSTRUCT_ARCHITECTURE: Both halves first built as one fused gene, in both orders; neither worked (data not shown), so two separate plasmids were used [Discussion, p. 3721].

title: Improvement of heterologous protein production in Aspergillus oryzae by RNA interference with alpha-amylase genes
authors: Nemoto T; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: The fungus naturally releases large amounts of amylase, an enzyme that breaks down starch. Researchers used RNA interference to turn down several amylase genes without deleting them. Amylase activity fell while production of chymosin (used to make cheese) increased. The idea that less amylase freed up production capacity is plausible, but was not directly proven.
notes: Results text reports chymosin in mg/ml while Fig. 3 uses ug/ml; the figure is correct, so values here are mg/L. Results says amylase activity "decreased by 30-40%" but the Discussion says "reduced to 30-40%", which the figure confirms; the Discussion wording is the accurate one. Only the chymosin control (69.8) and range (89.7-109.6) are text-stated; the strain values are read from the figures. Chymosin is the average of nine experiments; amylase of three. Lower amylase activity is the intended effect: freeing secretion capacity for chymosin is the authors' proposed explanation, not a demonstrated mechanism, and CHY mRNA was unchanged (Fig. 4).

title: Comparative genomic analysis identified a mutation related to enhanced heterologous protein production in the filamentous fungus Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Jin FJ; Katayama T; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers investigated an unusually productive fungal mutant by comparing its DNA with that of its parent strain. They identified a change in a gene called autA, then showed that recreating the change or deleting the gene increased human lysozyme production. The gene's normal function, and why changing it helps, remain unclear.
notes: Table 2 names the control strain SlD-HLY while Fig. 5's legend calls it SlD-HLY1; rows here follow Table 2. Parent NSPlD1 has no protease deletions, unlike the AUT1 lineage this work came from, so these yields are not comparable to Nemoto 2009's. AutA is an uncharacterized predicted hydrolase; why the mutation raises yield is unknown. Supplementary Fig. S3 repeats the mutation in a protease-deficient background (NSlD-tApE), with growth slightly delayed and HLY lower in the first 24 h.

title: Overexpression of msnA reprograms metabolism to enhance recombinant protein secretion across Aspergillus species
authors: Antoniel EP; Bernardi JV; Wassano NS; Gerhardt JA; Rodrigues AG; de Figueiredo FL; Morera-Gomez M; Mortensen UH; Damasio A
summary: Researchers added genes from a related fungus that control the activity of many other genes. In A. oryzae, adding msnA increased the target-protein signal compared with the amount of all protein secreted. Adding crzA raised that ratio mainly because total secreted protein fell, not because much more target protein was released. These results are not the same as higher target-protein concentrations.
notes: Only the A. oryzae arms are curated; the paper's headline 2.8-fold is A. nidulans at 72 h, while Fig. 2B gives 1.73x for A. niger and 1.52x for A. oryzae. msnA and crzA are A. nidulans genes under A. nidulans promoters and terminators, so these are foreign transcription factors rather than extra copies of the host's own, and their gene IDs will be A. nidulans identifiers rather than AO090 tags. The cargo in both mCitrine arms is a native A. oryzae gene (AO090012000046) carrying a fluorescent tag; only the AbfA arm has a foreign cargo. Every cargo value is normalized per total protein, so vs_control is a ratio of ratios, not comparable to the mg/L fold changes elsewhere. The only absolute amounts are the Bradford totals in Fig. 4B. The dataset has no field marking measurement basis, which this paper, PANCHANAWAPORN2026 and NEMOTO2009RNAI all need; that question is still open.

title: Using DNA-tagged mutagenesis to improve heterologous protein production in Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Yaver DS; Lamsa M; Munds R; Brown SH; Otani S; Franssen L; Johnstone JA; Brody H
summary: Researchers inserted pieces of DNA into many fungal strains to disrupt genes at different locations, then screened for strains that released more lipase, an enzyme that breaks down fats. This led them to palB, a gene involved in sensing the acidity of the environment. Disrupting it improved relative lipase activity but also caused problems with growth under alkaline conditions.
notes: Relative lipase activity only; no actual amount reported. Both arms inherit amyA/amyB/amyC mutations; disruption introduces pyrG into the pyrG-mutant parent. Disruptants cannot grow on minimal-medium plates at pH 8. Table 4 gives 2.0-2.1x at day 8, but p. 33 says 30-40% more; table values retained.

title: Isolation of Aspergillus oryzae mutants for heterologous protein production from a double proteinase gene disruptant
authors: Nemoto T; Watanabe T; Mizogami Y; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers rebuilt a strain with two protein-destroying genes disabled and confirmed that it produced more chymosin, an enzyme used to make cheese. They then used ultraviolet light to create random mutations and selected strains making more human lysozyme and chymosin. The extra mutations responsible for those gains were not identified in this paper.
notes: Created NS-tApE, the host used in NEMOTO2009RNAI and JIN2016. Double tppA/pepE disruption improved chymosin as well as the earlier lysozyme result. Additional AUT gains from UV mutagenesis are not curated because their causal mutations were unidentified in this paper.

title: Both Galactosaminogalactan and α-1,3-Glucan Contribute to Aggregation of Aspergillus oryzae Hyphae in Liquid Culture
authors: Miyazawa K; Yoshimi A; Sano M; Tabata F; Sugahara A; Kasahara S; Koizumi A; Yano S; Nakajima T; Abe K
summary: In liquid culture, this fungus forms clumps that can restrict growth. Researchers disrupted genes involved in making two sticky cell-surface materials so its threads grew more separately. The modified strain released more CutL1, an enzyme naturally made by the fungus, but also grew substantially more biomass. The results do not establish that each unit of fungus became better at secreting protein.
notes: Cargo is CutL1, A. oryzae's own cutinase overexpressed from a strong promoter, not a foreign protein. The text's "approximately 10 times" and "4 times" are the biomass folds (Fig. 9C), not the CutL1 folds, which are 6.65x and 2.97x (Fig. 9D). CutL1 per unit biomass fell about 39% in both mutants, so the gain comes from growing more fungus rather than better secretion per cell; that ratio is derived here, not stated by the paper. No strain with the GAG deletions alone was tested for production. Both mutants are significantly more sensitive to cell-wall-degrading enzymes and Congo Red (Fig. 3). All values read from figures; the text gives none. The ags strains were built in Miyazawa 2016, so check for overlap before curating that paper.

title: Engineering Aspergillus oryzae for enhanced heterologous protein production by synthetic biology toolkit development and morphology control
authors: Huang Q; Huang K; Wang B; Pan L
summary: Researchers developed tools to make genetic edits in Aspergillus oryzae more easily. They then disrupted a gene called chsY, changing how the fungal threads grow and making the liquid culture less thick. That change improved the release of a recombinant lipase, an enzyme that breaks down fats.

title: Improved recombinant protein production in Aspergillus oryzae lacking both α-1,3-glucan and galactosaminogalactan in batch culture with a lab-scale bioreactor
authors: Ichikawa H; Miyazawa K; Komeiji K; Susukida S; Zhang S; Muto K; Orita R; Takeuchi A; Kamachi Y; Hitosugi M; Yoshimi A; Shintani T; Kato Y; Abe K
summary: Researchers tested whether preventing fungal clumps still helped protein production in a stirred fermentation tank. They compared strains missing either or both of two sticky cell-surface materials. The strain missing both released the most CutL1, an enzyme naturally made by the fungus, even though the strains had similar amounts of fungal growth. Its liquid culture was also less thick at high stirring speeds.

title: Increased enzyme production under liquid culture conditions in the industrial fungus Aspergillus oryzae by disruption of the genes encoding cell wall α-1,3-glucan synthase
authors: Miyazawa K; Yoshimi A; Zhang S; Sano M; Nakayama M; Gomi K; Abe K
summary: Researchers disabled three genes used to make a sticky material on the fungus's cell wall, causing smaller clumps in liquid culture. They then tested production of CutL1, an enzyme naturally made by the fungus, and found that more was released as the modified strain grew more biomass. An additional strain with further deletions offered no clear improvement over the first modified strain.
notes: May report the same CutL1 experiments as the 2019 study; check for overlap before curating either.

title: Construction of Quintuple Protease and Double Amylase Gene Deletant for Heterologous Protein Production in Aspergillus oryzae KBN616
authors: Kitamoto N; Ono N; Yoshino-Yasuda S
summary: Researchers removed several genes for protein-destroying and starch-digesting enzymes from an industrial strain of A. oryzae. The modified fungus released far less of these native enzymes, potentially making it a cleaner host for manufacturing other proteins. The researchers did not actually measure production of an added target protein in the final strain.
notes: Host is A. oryzae KBN616, not a RIB40 derivative. Combines protease deletion with amylase deletion in one strain. Different group from the Kitamoto K lab that produced most other rows here; do not confuse the two.

title: Modulating endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi cargo receptors for improving secretion of carrier-fused heterologous proteins in the filamentous fungus Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Hoang HD; Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers disrupted two genes for receptors that help move proteins through the fungus. Each change increased release of chymosin (used to make cheese) and a glowing test protein, with less product stuck inside the cell. However, disrupting Aovip36 also reduced secretion of the fungus's own amylase, showing that an edit can help one product while hurting another.
notes: Every production number is a figure bar (n=3); the only one written out is "approximately 2-fold" for chymosin. In both deletion strains less of each product stayed stuck in the ER (Fig. 5), matching the higher secretion. One copy of the product gene at niaD in every strain, confirmed by Southern blot. Table 1 spells some strains three ways (NSlD1 / NSPlD1 / NSlD-1); names here follow Table 1.

title: Multiple gene disruptions by marker recycling with highly efficient gene-targeting background (ΔligD) in Aspergillus oryzae
authors: Maruyama J; Kitamoto K
summary: Researchers developed a way to disable several fungal genes in sequence, reusing the same DNA marker after each change. They demonstrated the method by removing protein-destroying genes in a strain engineered for more precise gene editing. The paper does not report a new comparison of secreted target-protein production.

title: Improved recombinant protein production and scale-up fermentation of Aspergillus oryzae hyphal-dispersion hydrophobin-deficient strain
authors: Susukida S; Baba Y; Fujisawa M; Niikawa Y; Muto K; Miyazawa K; Yoshimi A; Kato Y; Horiguchi H; Abe K
summary: Earlier work made fungal threads grow separately, but they still stuck to fermentation equipment. Researchers disabled rolA, a gene for a water-repelling surface protein, to reduce this sticking. The strain showed better enzyme production in smaller experiments and was also tested in larger fermentation tanks, where liquid flow improved. These findings are from a preprint, not yet a peer-reviewed paper.

title: Method for constructing recombinant Aspergillus oryzae strain
authors: Lin J; Zhang G; Zheng F
summary: This patent application describes removing pacG, a possible gene regulator, from a fungus engineered to make human lactoferrin, a protein found in milk. The applicant measured lactoferrin in the culture liquid using a laboratory separation method called HPLC and reported more after the edit. Some culture conditions and the assay are described, but replicate counts and independent confirmation are not established.
notes: Curation candidate: pacG knockout by CRISPR against an existing human-lactoferrin-producing parent. Patent reports 0.02 mg/mL for control AO-huLF869 and 0.23 mg/mL for AO-pacG759, i.e. 20 and 230 mg/L; the 11.5x is a ratio of those two values rather than a figure the document states, so keep it out of any outcomes row. Not peer reviewed, and conditions, replicates and assay are not established. Applicant Nanjing Bestzyme Bioengineering.
